cases.note: A recursive walk never names its files as operands, so the routing reconcile never sees them; the cached copy must be checked where it is served. The two named cats warm the cache first, because grep -r fills none of its own and would read cold either way. Narrowed to the backends that may declare `read: fresh`: the other five cache reads but stamp no comparable content token, so the mount-time verdict refuses the policy and the workspace never constructs. The bounded control keeps the full list.

The control for the `fresh` twin: the walk really does read the warm cache, so under `bounded` it serves the stale copy. Without this, the `fresh` case could pass because the walk never touched the cache at all. It runs on all seven targets where its twin runs on two, because `bounded` is allowed everywhere.

A glob expands after routing, so its files are never named operands and the pre-command reconcile skips them; the copy is checked where it is served. Narrowed to the backends that may declare `read: fresh`: the other five cache reads but stamp no comparable content token, so the mount-time verdict refuses the policy and the workspace never constructs. The bounded control keeps the full list.

A line spanning two mounts fans out per mount, so the walk of /data2 runs under that mount's own cache manager rather than the single-mount routing path; its files are never named operands and the cached copy must be checked where it is served. A named cat of the same files across sibling mounts would not do: named operands were already reconciled at routing. Narrowed to the backends that may declare `read: fresh`: the other five cache reads but stamp no comparable content token, so the mount-time verdict refuses the policy and the workspace never constructs. The bounded control keeps the full list.
